summary: The manuscript fits a random-matrix risk model to ridge/PLS learning curves on 38 spectroscopic calibration tasks. It proposes regularisation-path matching (RPM) for pilot-based forecasting, and ends by recommending a simple rule: the pilot CV error plus a transferred slope of about 8.3% per doubling (SLOPE-T), with leave-one-source-out calibrated bands. The in-distribution comparison is careful and the raw outputs are complete; I could reproduce Table 4 and the pooled 79.3% coverage exactly. From a robustness and generalisation standpoint, however, the recommended toolkit is not supported outside the in-distribution soil setting. (1) SLOPE-T, RPM-w and the calibrated bands were never run in the robustness and shift experiments. Recomputing SLOPE-T from the stored outputs shows it is second-worst under the new-season shift (|log err| 0.489, 63% optimistic) and worse than FLAT under added reference noise. (2) The 'leave-one-source-out' transfer treats KSSL and Neospectra as independent, although they share the same soils and reference values. With them merged, SLOPE-T is no longer better than RPM, RPM-w or FLAT, and a cross-domain slope prior more than doubles its error on soils. (3) 'Nominal' calibrated-band coverage is a pooled average in which 84% of forecasts are soil. Coverage is 29–50% for mixtures, pharma and fuel, 46–57% at 128–256×, and 71% task-averaged. (4) The constant-slope rule's optimism grows steadily with the extrapolation ratio, reaching -0.39 log units at 256×. (5) Shift evidence comes from one data set and omits the key practical finding that the curve is flat under a new season; clustered or convenience pilots, geographic and instrument shifts are untested. (6) The robustness runs change the test split and pilots relative to the main study, have no baseline row and no uncertainty estimates. (7) Title, Significance and Conclusions generalise beyond linear calibration. Further concerns: the Kennard–Stone truth mismatch, designed and small sets, ground-truth noise, an unrealistic noise model, reduced spectral resolution and log-scale targets. Most issues can be fixed by reanalysis of existing outputs plus modest additional experiments, but the practical recommendations must be re-derived and qualified.
strengths: Robustness and shift experiments were pre-registered (E7), executed and reported, including unfavourable results and an explicit 'compensating biases, not skill' caveat for the mango season shift.
Complete per-forecast raw outputs (raw_results.csv, robustness_raw.csv, truth_*.npz) made independent recomputation possible. Table 4 and the pooled LOSO-conformal coverage (79.3%) reproduce exactly.

The Limitations section openly acknowledges the linear-only scope, the random-sampling premise and the soil dominance of the task set, even though the Abstract and Conclusions do not carry these qualifiers through.
Group-disjoint splitting, replicate averaging and the identifiability analysis of the noise floor are carefully done, and the negative RPM-T result is reported rather than tuned away.

issues.title: The recommended planning toolkit (SLOPE-T, RPM-w, calibrated bands) was never tested under any robustness or shift scenario, and recomputation shows SLOPE-T fails under a new season and under noisier reference values
issues.description: Abstract, Conclusions and Section 4.10 (ii), (iii) and (vi) recommend the pilot CV error plus a transferred slope of about 8.3% per doubling (SLOPE-T), RPM-w where no prior calibrations exist, and leave-one-source-out calibrated bands. Table 4 (Section 4.8) and Table S25 report only RPM, RPM-T, RPM-wT, IPL3 and FLAT. The code hard-wires this: experiments/robustness.py, KEEP = ["RPM", "RPM-T", "RPM-wT", "IPL3", "FLAT"]. RPM-w and the calibrated bands are therefore not evaluated outside the in-distribution main study. SLOPE-T can be computed exactly from the stored FLAT rows, as in experiments/analysis.py::add_slope_transfer. Doing so reverses the paper's message for two of the seven scenarios. In the new-season mango shift, SLOPE-T is the second-worst method (optimistic by a factor of exp(0.489) = 1.63) while RPM is the best. Under added reference noise, SLOPE-T is clearly worse than FLAT because a slope transferred from cleaner calibrations is too steep. The recommended rule is thus fragile in exactly the conditions where planning matters: a different reference laboratory or noisier method, and a new season or population. The manuscript's statement that forecasts 'do not transfer across shifts' is generic and gives no numbers for the methods it recommends.
issues.evidence: My recomputation from results/robustness_raw.csv (per-task mean |log err| (mean bias); SLOPE-T = FLAT + LOSO slope from results/slope_per_doubling.csv × log2(n/n0)). Mango new season: SLOPE-T 0.489 (-0.489), FLAT 0.250, RPM 0.115, IPL3 1.034. Reference noise: SLOPE-T 0.191 (-0.156) vs FLAT 0.129. SG1: SLOPE-T 0.367 (-0.252) vs FLAT 0.313. Raw absorbance: SLOPE-T 0.240 vs FLAT 0.201. KS pilots: SLOPE-T 0.240 (+0.055). Mango populations: SLOPE-T 0.121. My values for the reported methods reproduce Table 4 exactly (e.g. raw: RPM 0.274, FLAT 0.201, IPL3 0.405). RPM 80% bootstrap coverage drops from 48% (my recomputed in-distribution baseline on the same 6 tasks, n0 ∈ {50,100}, pilots 0–9) to 6–36% in six of seven scenarios (Table 4).
issues.corrective_action: Add SLOPE-T, RPM-w and the LOSO-conformal bands of every method to Table 4, Table S25 and Fig. 10, with an in-distribution baseline row. Rewrite Section 4.8 and recommendations (ii), (iii) and (vi) to state explicitly that the transferred-slope rule becomes optimistic, by tens of percent, under season shift and when the reference method is noisier than in the calibrations the slope came from. Remove 'sound planning rule' from the Significance statement or qualify it with these conditions.
issues.proposed_experiment: Rerun E7 with RPM-w added to KEEP and with SLOPE-T and LOSO-conformal bands computed for every scenario. Use the main-study test split and pilot seeds; see issue R6-C01-07. Report coverage of the calibrated bands under each shift.

issues.title: 'Leave-one-source-out' transfer is not leave-one-domain-out: KSSL and Neospectra share the same soils and reference values. With the correct source definition, SLOPE-T is no longer better than RPM or FLAT
issues.description: SLOPE-T, RPM-T and the calibrated bands are justified as transfer from other data sources. However, experiments/analysis.py::source_of (line 48) and experiments/refinement.py::source_of (line 23) treat 'KSSL' and 'Neospectra' as separate sources. The Neospectra library is a re-scan of KSSL archive soils. Its site file carries the KSSL layer ID, and the reference values are the KSSL laboratory values. The paper itself shows that the slope is governed mainly by the noise fraction, which is a property of the reference values. Transferring a slope from KSSL to Neospectra therefore transfers the answer. Once the 12 KSSL and Neospectra tasks are treated as one source, the 'most accurate method overall' claim (Section 4.3; Abstract) disappears. A further check shows the 'typical slope' is strongly domain-specific. If a soil laboratory used the slope median of the non-soil calibrations (-0.195), SLOPE-T's error on soil tasks would more than double. The transfer works here only because 23 of 38 tasks, and 84% of forecasts, are soils with similar slopes.
issues.evidence: data_raw/ossl/Neospectra/ossl_soilsite_v1.3.csv.gz, column id.kssl.lay_local_txt: 2,084 of 2,106 Neospectra samples match KSSL id.layer_local_c, and all 2,084 have KSSL MIR spectra in code/data/cache/ossl_KSSL_mir.npz. Reference values are identical for 96.4% (OC), 96.2% (clay) and 100% (pH) of the matched samples. My recomputation from results/raw_results.csv with KSSL and Neospectra merged into one source: SLOPE-T mean task error 0.262 (paper 0.251; Neospectra 0.190→0.220, KSSL 0.251→0.288). Versus RPM: median paired difference -0.014, better on 21/38 tasks, unadjusted Wilcoxon p = 0.18 (paper: Holm p = 0.031, 25/38). Versus FLAT: 19/38, p = 0.67. Versus RPM-w: p = 0.40. With a cross-domain prior (soil tasks receive the median slope of non-soil tasks, -0.195), SLOPE-T on soil rises from 0.208 to 0.475.
issues.corrective_action: Redefine sources so that libraries sharing samples or reference laboratories are grouped: KSSL with Neospectra, and also check AfSIS and ICRAF laboratory overlap. Recompute SLOPE-T, RPM-T priors, LOSO-conformal bands and all Holm tests. Add a leave-one-application-domain-out analysis (soil vs fruit, fuel, pharma, meat and mixtures). Soften the Abstract claim that a transferred slope was 'equally accurate', and state in Section 4.10 that the prior must come from calibrations of the same application domain and reference method.

issues.title: 'Nominal coverage' of the calibrated bands is a soil-weighted pooled average; outside soils and at long horizons the bands under-cover severely
issues.description: Abstract ('Bands calibrated across data sets reached nominal coverage') and Section 4.5 report coverage pooled over forecasts. 84.1% of the 10,700 forecasts per method come from soil tasks, because these have the most horizons. Section 3.7 declares the task to be the unit of analysis, but coverage is not reported per task or per family. Recomputed with the paper's own algorithm, the claimed 'honest 80% bands spanning a factor of about 1.77' hold for soils only. The tasks most like a new application (fuel, pharma, designed mixtures) and the long horizons (128–256×) are badly under-covered.
issues.evidence: Replicating experiments/analysis.py lines 382–404 on results/raw_results.csv reproduces the pooled 79.3% (SLOPE-T 80% band). By family: soil 83.6%, fruit 88.9%, meat 76.1%, fuel 49.6%, pharma 37.5%, mixtures 28.8%. RPM-w: pharma 33.0%, fuel 54.9%, mixtures 56.7%. Task-averaged coverage is 71.0% (SLOPE-T) and 74.3% (RPM-w). By extrapolation ratio, SLOPE-T coverage is 56.6% at 128× and 45.6% at 256×. Eight tasks have coverage below 60% (minimum Diesel:total 5.8%).
issues.corrective_action: Report coverage per task (task-averaged), per family and per ratio bin in Table S20 and Fig. 8. Replace 'reached nominal coverage' in the Abstract with a statement restricted to soil spectral libraries. Consider Mondrian (family-wise) or task-weighted conformal calibration, and state that bands calibrated on one application domain cannot be assumed valid for another.

issues.title: The constant 'about 8.3% per doubling' rule is systematically and increasingly optimistic for long extrapolations, and long-horizon evidence comes from 8–17 soil-dominated tasks
issues.description: Section 4.2 derives the 8.3% figure from an OLS slope of log RMSE on log2 n over the whole ground-truth curve. That curve spans 50–100 for Tecator and CGL but 50–6400 for KSSL. Real curves are strongly concave in log-log coordinates, so the 'slope per doubling' depends on the n-range and is not a constant. Applied as a constant from the pilot size, the rule becomes more optimistic the longer the extrapolation. Section 4.3 states that 'the same three methods led at short and long extrapolations alike'. That masks opposite, growing biases: FLAT is pessimistic and SLOPE-T optimistic by roughly 0.3 log units at ≥64×. It is not a case of accurate forecasting. Long-horizon claims also rest on few tasks: ≥16× on 25 tasks (23 soil, mango, tablets), ≥64× on 17 (16 soil, mango), and ≥128× on the 8 KSSL tasks only.
issues.evidence: My recomputation from results/raw_results.csv, SLOPE-T mean signed log error by ratio: 2× -0.106, 4× -0.091, 8× -0.132, 16× -0.178, 32× -0.219, 64× -0.264, 128× -0.328, 256× -0.386. At ratio ≥64 (17 tasks): SLOPE-T bias -0.299, optimistic on 16/17 tasks, only 24% of forecasts within ±20%; FLAT bias +0.330. From n0 = 200 at 32× (n = 6400) the bias is -0.261. Local slopes from results/raw/truth_*.npz: KSSL-VisNIR:OC -0.302 (50→100) to -0.017 (3200→6400); KSSL-MIR:OC -0.120 to -0.004; Mango:DM -0.096 to -0.017; Neospectra-NIR:OC -0.260 to -0.018.
issues.corrective_action: Report the signed bias of every method by extrapolation ratio and by absolute n (main text, not only Fig. 6). Replace the constant slope with an n-dependent slope, e.g. a slope prior indexed by the n-interval, or a slope that decays with log n as implied by Eq. (3). Alternatively, restrict recommendation (ii) to ≤16× extrapolations and state that the rule overestimates gains beyond a few hundred samples. State in the Abstract and Limitations which tasks support each extrapolation range.

issues.title: Distribution-shift evidence rests on one data set, the shift-induced plateau is not drawn out, and realistic non-random pilots (clustered or convenience campaigns, new region, new instrument) are not tested
issues.description: All shift results (Table 4, rows 'Mango: …') come from a single fruit data set. No soil, instrument or geographic shift was run, although the data allow it. OSSL contains per-instrument Neospectra scans that were averaged away (datasets.py::_read_ossl keeps only 'Multiple' rows). KSSL and AfSIS carry site, region or country information. The most important practical finding of the season experiment is not stated: under a new season the true learning curve is flat, so additional calibration samples from old seasons buy almost nothing. A rule forecasting 8.3% per doubling (or RPM) is then structurally wrong. Recommendation (v) ('use random pilot sets from the target population') is often infeasible at the planning stage, because a pilot is typically the first campaign, a few sites, one orchard or one season. That clustered-pilot case was never simulated: in the main study pilots are drawn uniformly from the whole pool, spanning all seasons and sites.
issues.evidence: Truth curves extracted from results/robustness_raw.csv. Mango new season: RMSE 1.499 (n=100), 1.397 (200), 1.355 (400), 1.346 (800), 1.339 (1600), local slopes -0.071, -0.031, -0.007, -0.006 per doubling. The i.i.d. reference from seasons 1–3 falls to 0.934 at n=1600. Under the new season, FLAT bias -0.250 and SLOPE-T bias -0.489 (my recomputation). The 'shift' scenarios use one task (Table 4 n_tasks = 1). The main-study pilot sampling is in src/evaluation/forecast_experiment.py::run_pilots (rng.choice(pool, n0)).
issues.corrective_action: Discuss explicitly that under shift the slope approaches zero, so pilot-based slope forecasts and RPM are invalid regardless of their in-distribution accuracy. Downgrade recommendation (v) to a stated assumption with its practical cost. Add shift experiments in at least two further domains before claiming that forecasts 'do not transfer across shifts' in general, or that the methods behave as described under shift.
issues.proposed_experiment: (a) Clustered pilots: draw each pilot from k ∈ {1, 3, 5} random sites (soil) or one season or population (mango), and forecast the random-calibration truth of the whole population. (b) Geographic shift: KSSL or AfSIS pilots and pools from a subset of regions or countries, tested on held-out regions. (c) Instrument shift: Neospectra single-instrument pilots forecasting a different-instrument test set. Evaluate RPM, RPM-w, FLAT, SLOPE-T and calibrated bands, with 20 pilots per n0.

issues.title: Conclusions overgeneralise beyond linear calibration and beyond the scenarios where power-law extrapolation was actually tested
issues.description: The title ('multivariate calibration learning curves'), the Significance statement ('Calibration learning curves are governed by the spectral eigen-structure and the noise floor. Power-law extrapolation from small pilot sets should be abandoned') and the first sentence of the Conclusions ('Learning curves of multivariate calibrations are not arbitrary') are unqualified. The evidence covers only ridge and PLS1. Section 2.1 defines σ² to include 'any non-linearity that a linear calibration cannot capture', so the 'noise floor' that governs the slope is a linear-model floor, not an irreducible one. For non-linear analytes, and for large libraries such as KSSL where local, Cubist or deep models are standard (ref. [5]), the attainable floor and slope differ. The qualifier appears only in Limitation 1. The pre-registration (RQ5) promised robustness to 'model family', but this was delivered only as a PLS truth. 'Should be abandoned' is also contradicted by the paper's own data: IPL3 was the most accurate method with Kennard–Stone pilots and in the misspecified simulation. Finally, IPL was tested only on ridge regression, not on the classification setting of ref. [8].
issues.evidence: Table 4: KS pilots IPL3 0.316 vs RPM 0.363 and FLAT 0.330. Section 4.7: at r = 0.5, IPL3 0.197 vs RPM 0.221. Supplementary Table S2/T9: Tecator:fat, a classic non-linear NIR analyte, has a theory-fit error of 0.177, twice the median of 0.087, even though only two truth points (n = 50, 100) are fitted. Diesel:total has 0.378. Section 2.1 gives the definition of σ². supplementary/EXPERIMENT_DESIGN_preregistration.md RQ5 includes 'model family'.
issues.corrective_action: Qualify the title or abstract ('linear (ridge/PLS) calibration'). Restrict the Significance and Conclusions statements to linear calibrations of regression targets. Replace 'should be abandoned' with 'performed worse than simple anchored rules in most in-distribution settings tested here'. State that the 8.3% rule describes linear-model gains only and may underestimate gains of non-linear or local models.
issues.proposed_experiment: Optional but recommended to substantiate RQ5 'model family': compute truth curves for a non-linear learner (e.g. RBF kernel ridge, Cubist or memory-based learning, or a small 1D-CNN) on KSSL-MIR OC/clay (up to 6400) and Tecator fat. Test whether FLAT, SLOPE-T (with the ridge-derived slope) and RPM forecasts remain accurate.

issues.title: Robustness experiment is confounded and under-powered: variants change the test split and pilots, Table 4 has no baseline row, there is no uncertainty quantification, and the pre-processing variants are atypical
issues.description: (a) Confounding. In experiments/robustness.py the pre-processing and noise variants rename the task ('[raw]', '[sg1]', '[+noise]') before run_truth/run_pilots. Both the test split and the pilot seeds are derived from task_seed(task.name) (src/evaluation/forecast_experiment.py), so each variant has a different, essentially random test set and different pilots. Differences from the main study, and between variants, mix the effect of the perturbation with split-to-split variation. That variation is large for the small sets (test sets of 95–164). (b) Table 4 has no in-distribution reference row for the same six tasks, n0 and pilots, so the reader cannot see what each perturbation does. (c) Six tasks × 10 pilots, with no CIs or tests: with six paired tasks, the smallest attainable two-sided Wilcoxon p is 0.031, so no Holm-corrected statement is possible. (d) SG1 is applied with an 11-point window after sub-sampling (src/preprocessing/spectra.py). That is 100 nm on VisNIR, 160 cm⁻¹ on MIR and 80 nm on Neospectra, a heavy smoothing rarely used in practice. The common SNV+derivative ('snv_sg1', implemented) and MSC or detrend were not run.
issues.evidence: I recomputed the test-set overlap of each variant with the main split using the code's split_task and task_seed: Diesel:bp50 21% / 34% / 26% ([raw] / [sg1] / [+noise]), Tablets:assay 27% / 27% / 24%, Mango:DM 25% / 24% / 26%, i.e. chance level (~25%). Recomputed baseline (main study, SNV, random pilots, same 6 tasks, n0 ∈ {50,100}, pilots 0–9): RPM 0.237, RPM-w 0.240, FLAT 0.199, SLOPE-T 0.204, IPL3 0.454, RPM 80% coverage 48%. So SG1 raises RPM error by +0.13 and FLAT by +0.11, but by how much of that is split variation cannot be told. code/config/full.yaml: robustness n_pilots 10, n0_list [50, 100].
issues.corrective_action: Seed the split and pilots from the base task name in every variant, so that only the perturbation differs. Add the baseline row and per-scenario paired differences with pilot- or task-bootstrap CIs. Increase to ≥12 tasks and 20 pilots. Add SNV+SG1 (window ≈ 11–25 nm at native resolution) and MSC.
issues.proposed_experiment: Re-run E7 with fixed base seeds, ≥12 tasks covering all families, 20 pilots and n0 ∈ {25, 50, 100, 200}, adding SNV+SG1 and MSC. Report paired differences against the in-distribution baseline with CIs.

issues.title: The Kennard–Stone scenario scores KS pilots against a random-calibration truth, so recommendation (v) is not established
issues.description: In practice, a laboratory that selects its pilot by Kennard–Stone would normally select the full calibration set the same way. The relevant truth is the error of KS-designed calibrations of size n. The code instead reuses the main-study random-calibration truth ('identical split & truth as the main study'), and draws the KS pilot from only 10·n0 random candidates. The large positive bias of RPM and FLAT may therefore partly reflect this truth mismatch rather than a failure of pilot-based forecasting. Moreover, the recommended SLOPE-T was the most accurate method under KS pilots, again through compensating biases. The blanket statement that space-filling selections 'bias every pilot-based forecast' and 'should not be used' is not supported as written.
issues.evidence: experiments/robustness.py, ks_pilot branch: truth = run_truth(...) with the comment '# identical split & truth as the main study'; cand = rng.choice(pool, min(len(pool), 10 * n0)). Table 4 KS row: RPM 0.363 (+0.33), FLAT 0.330 (+0.30), IPL3 0.316. My recomputation: SLOPE-T 0.240 (+0.055).
issues.corrective_action: Add a truth curve for KS-designed calibrations (KS selection of n from the pool, or from a candidate set of fixed size) and evaluate KS-pilot forecasts against it. Rephrase recommendation (v) accordingly.
issues.proposed_experiment: For the six robustness tasks, compute ground-truth curves for KS-selected calibration sets at each n. Re-score KS-pilot forecasts of all methods against both the random-design and KS-design truth.

issues.title: Small and designed data sets: the recommended rule breaks for designed mixtures and pharma, and these sets support only 2–4× extrapolations
issues.description: CGL designed mixtures have slopes 3–6× the median and a fitted noise fraction of about 1e-4 (gravimetric references). Here both anchored rules are strongly pessimistic and FLAT is the worst non-curve method. On Tablets every method is optimistic. Section 4.10 (ii) only says the slope is 'less when the reference method is noisy'. It does not warn that the slope is much steeper for designed or low-noise data. Tecator and CGL (7 of 38 tasks) have only horizons n = 50 and 100, i.e. ratios 2–4×, so they cannot test long extrapolation at all. The theory's in-sample fit to two points still misses by 0.29–0.33 for CGL lactate and moisture.
issues.evidence: results/slope_per_doubling.csv: CGL -0.254 to -0.528, Diesel:d4052 -0.428. tables/T9_theory_validity_full_pool_fit.md: CGL noise_frac 1.4–2.6e-4, theory error 0.330 and 0.287. Per-family recomputation from results/raw_results.csv (mean task |log err| (bias)): mixtures SLOPE-T 0.350 (+0.297), FLAT 0.437 (+0.409), RPM 0.311, IPL3 0.336. Pharma: FLAT 0.327 (-0.114), SLOPE-T 0.393 (-0.287), RPM 0.474 (-0.335). tables/T1_tasks.md: max n = 100 for Tecator and CGL.
issues.corrective_action: State in Section 4.10 and the Conclusions that the transferred-slope rule does not apply to designed experiments or to references with near-zero error. Report the family-level table (T11) with SLOPE-T and RPM-w included in the main text. Consider conditioning the slope prior on the known precision of the reference method, which is often known a priori even if the pilot cannot estimate it.

issues.title: Ground-truth uncertainty is ignored, and several truth curves are non-monotone or dominated by Monte-Carlo and test-set noise
issues.description: Each task uses one fixed test split (Limitation 5), and the truth is the mean test MSE over 8–30 repetitions. For the small sets, test-set sampling error alone is comparable to the between-method differences on which conclusions are drawn (0.01–0.03), and is a sizeable fraction of the forecast errors themselves (~0.2–0.4). At n = 100, the CGL and Tecator calibrations are drawn from pools of only 173–180 samples, so repetitions overlap heavily. Six of 38 truth curves are non-monotone, with the mean dominated by occasional tuning failures. Diesel:total has a positive slope (+0.117), which enters the LOSO slope pool, and it is the worst-covered task for the calibrated bands. None of this uncertainty is propagated into the task-level errors or the Wilcoxon tests.
issues.evidence: results/raw/truth_*.npz: test sizes CGL 58, Tecator 60, Diesel 95–99, Tablets 164. Approximate SE of log RMSE ≈ 1/sqrt(2·n_test) = 0.093, 0.091, 0.071 and 0.055. Diesel:total ridge RMSE 2.203→2.770→2.782 (n = 50, 100, 200), relative SE of mean MSE 0.20–0.25. AfSIS1-MIR:pH 0.554→0.635 (200→400; PLS decreases). KSSL-MIR:CEC 0.206→0.217 (1600→3200, relative SE 0.143 with 8 repetitions). ICRAF-VisNIR:OC, ICRAF-VisNIR:CEC and KSSL-VisNIR:clay also show local increases. Calibrated-band coverage for Diesel:total is 5.8% (SLOPE-T) and 4.2% (RPM-w), my recomputation.
issues.corrective_action: Use repeated group-disjoint test splits for all tasks with N < 1000. Report truth CIs and propagate them, e.g. by a bootstrap over repetitions and test samples within the task-level bootstrap. Add a sensitivity analysis that excludes non-monotone truth curves and uses a robust aggregate (median MSE over repetitions).
issues.proposed_experiment: For the 15 non-soil tasks, repeat the truth curve and pilot forecasts over ≥10 random group-disjoint test splits. Report the split-to-split SD of each method's task error and redo the paired tests.

issues.title: The reference-noise scenario is unrealistic and mislabelled, and the proposed noise-floor remedy is untested although the existing design could test it
issues.description: The noise scenario adds homoscedastic Gaussian noise to every label, test labels included, before splitting. It therefore represents 'a noisier reference method throughout', not noisy calibration labels scored against accurate validation values. It contains no gross errors (transcription or laboratory outliers) and no heteroscedastic (concentration-proportional) error. These are the common real cases, and RPM's least-squares log-path fit and RPM-w's weights from squared LOGO residuals are plausibly sensitive to a single gross error in a 25–50-sample pilot. Table 4 labels the scenario 'Reference noise +25%'. In fact the injected variance is 25% of var(y), which more than doubles σ² for a median task. The Conclusions propose replicate reference analyses as the route to better forecasts, but this is never tested, even though the noise scenario knows the injected variance exactly. It is also only a partial remedy: by Section 2.1, σ² also contains linear misfit, which replicates cannot measure.
issues.evidence: experiments/robustness.py, ref_noise branch: task.y = task.y + rng.normal(0, sqrt(noise_frac·var(y)), len(task.y)) on all samples. code/config/full.yaml noise_frac: 0.25. results/alignment_exponents.csv: median large-sample noise fraction 0.16. Table 4 row label 'Reference noise +25%'. My recomputation: SLOPE-T under this scenario 0.191 vs FLAT 0.129.
issues.corrective_action: Relabel the scenario ('added noise variance = 0.25·var(y)'). Discuss that gross errors and heteroscedastic noise were not tested. Either test the replicate remedy or present it explicitly as a conjecture, and note its limitation for non-linear analytes.
issues.proposed_experiment: (a) Noise in calibration labels only, with clean test labels. (b) 2–5% gross errors (±4 SD) in pilot labels. (c) Heteroscedastic noise proportional to y. (d) RPM/RPM-T with σ² lower-bounded by the known injected variance, as a direct test of the replicate-analysis remedy.

issues.title: Wavelength sub-sampling to p = 94–216 is a strong untested design choice that can affect the eigen-spectrum tail, the alignment exponents and late-curve saturation
issues.description: The theory and RPM depend on the eigen-spectrum, including weak modes, and Section 4.2 interprets r < 1 as signal in weak modes. Yet all spectra were sub-sampled 4–8× below the resolution in which they are distributed and used in practice. With p ≈ 200 and n up to 6400 (n/p ≈ 30), saturation of the learning curve is partly forced by the dimension cap, and the late flattening drives both the median slope and SLOPE-T's long-horizon bias. Neither the robustness study nor the ablation varies p, so it is unknown whether r, the κ-collapse, the slopes and the method ranking hold at native resolution.
issues.evidence: code/src/data/datasets.py OSSL_LIBS: steps of 10 nm (VisNIR), 16 cm⁻¹ (MIR) and 8 nm (Neospectra); load_diesel uses X[:, ::2] and load_tablets X[:, ::3]. Native OSSL files (data_raw/ossl/*): KSSL MIR 1,701 variables at 2 cm⁻¹, KSSL VisNIR 1,076 at 2 nm, Neospectra 601 at 2 nm. Table 1: p = 94–216.
issues.corrective_action: Justify the sub-sampling and add a sensitivity analysis on resolution. State in Limitations that results were obtained at reduced resolution.
issues.proposed_experiment: For 4–6 tasks (including KSSL-MIR OC and clay, which reach n = 6400), repeat the truth curves, the large-sample fits of r and σ², and RPM, RPM-w, SLOPE-T and FLAT forecasts at 2× finer and at native resolution.

issues.title: Log-transformed targets (11 tasks): errors, slopes and band widths are in log(1+y) units, not the units a planner uses
issues.description: OC and CEC were modelled as log(1+y), which partly linearises the problem. Planning targets are stated in original units (% OC, cmol/kg). Learning curves in original units are dominated by high-value samples and may have different slopes and noise floors. The pooled '8.3% per doubling' and 'factor 1.77' bands mix log-scale and linear-scale tasks without saying so in the recommendations.
issues.evidence: code/src/data/datasets.py OSSL_PROPS: OC and CEC 'log1p'. This affects 11 tasks (OC in six libraries, CEC in five). Section 3.1.
issues.corrective_action: Report the results for these 11 tasks separately, and either back-transform predictions to compute RMSE in original units or rerun them untransformed. Add a sentence to the Limitations.
issues.proposed_experiment: Recompute truth curves and forecasts for the 11 OC/CEC tasks on the original scale, or with back-transformed predictions, and compare slopes and method ranking.

issues.title: Factual inaccuracies in the description of the robustness results
issues.description: Section 4.8 says 'With orchard populations held out, all methods were pessimistic', but IPL3 was optimistic in that scenario (bias -0.285 in Table 4 itself). The Table 4 label 'Reference noise +25%' misstates the manipulation (see R6-C01-11). Section 4.8 also says that for the KS scenario 'IPL3's optimism happened to cancel this bias'. That is fair, but the same compensation explains SLOPE-T's good KS and population-shift results, so it should be described consistently once SLOPE-T is added.
issues.evidence: Table 4, row 'Mango: new populations': IPL3 0.440 (-0.28). Section 4.8, last paragraph.
issues.corrective_action: Correct the sentence to 'RPM, RPM-T and FLAT were pessimistic; IPL3 remained optimistic'. Fix the noise label. Describe compensating biases consistently for all methods.

recommendation_rationale: No single flaw invalidates the in-distribution findings on soil libraries. However, the paper's practical recommendations (transferred slope, calibrated bands, RPM-w as fallback) and its general claims about multivariate calibration rest on evidence that does not survive robustness checks. These include shift and noise scenarios in which the recommended rule was never run (and fails on recomputation), a source definition that leaks shared soils and reference values between 'independent' sources, coverage that holds only for soils and short horizons, and a constant slope that is increasingly optimistic at long horizons. Most corrections need reanalysis of existing outputs and a moderate set of new runs: fixed-seed E7 including SLOPE-T and RPM-w, clustered pilots, one more shift domain, and repeated splits for small sets. Claims must then be qualified to linear calibrations and to the domains where they were shown to hold.
